result:
The first time I noticed the ocean wasn’t really blue, it was because the sky had decided to be honest.

That morning, the light looked pale and undecided, like it couldn’t commit to one color without first checking with the clouds. I was standing on a low seawall behind a row of scrubby grass that never seemed to grow taller than my knees. The water was restless but not dramatic—small waves rolling in with the steady patience of something that had all the time in the world. I’d always thought of the ocean as one thing: blue, vast, and quiet. But under that shifting sky, it became layered, not with paint but with mood. It wasn’t just blue; it was green in places where the light thinned out, gray where the wind pressed its thumb against the surface, and almost black where the water swallowed shadows.

I remember thinking how strange it was that we call something “blue” when we can’t agree on what blue is. The word feels like a label we slap on the world to make it easier to carry. But the world rarely cooperates. It keeps insisting on detail.

After I watched for a while, I turned away from the water and walked along the path behind the houses. People were already outside. A woman was walking a dog that looked old in the gentle, unhurried way of creatures who have stopped trying to impress anyone. Someone was dragging a potted plant toward the light as if the day were something that could be rationed. In the windows, morning had made itself into reflections—squares of brightness floating atop glass. Everything had the careful feel of a day being assembled.

And yet, underneath it, there was the sense that I wasn’t just observing. I was being observed. The ocean, the sky, even the scruffy grass seemed to be paying attention to me in that wordless way nature has of acting like it’s not impressed by your existence but still makes room for you anyway.

That’s what the ocean does. It has a way of making you smaller without making you insignificant. You can stand there and feel humbled, and somehow it doesn’t feel like punishment. It’s more like being reminded that you’re a single instrument in a larger orchestra, that your notes matter, but only as part of a larger song.

I’ve had seasons in my life where I’ve needed that reminder. There are times when I feel too loud inside my own head—too crowded with worry, too busy being certain that the worst thing will happen because it’s the only thing that seems to make sense. In those seasons, I’m attracted to large, repetitive systems: rain, waves, the hum of traffic that turns individual cars into a single moving ribbon. Repetition is comforting. It doesn’t demand originality from me; it just keeps going.

On other days, I need the opposite: evidence that change exists and can be trusted. Those are the days I walk somewhere new or read something unfamiliar and feel my assumptions shift like sand. Change can be frightening because it means the old map no longer works. But change can also be thrilling because it suggests there might be another route through the same landscape.

The strange thing is that both kinds of days—the days I crave repetition and the days I want novelty—make me think of the same idea. Life is not a straight line. It’s more like tide. The water retreats, returns, retreats again, each movement different but clearly connected to the others.

When I was younger, I believed in progress as if it were a ladder: climb, reach, succeed, arrive. I thought you would know when you’d made it because something would feel permanent. Work would stabilize. Love would stay. Your body would hold its shape as though it owed you continuity. I thought the future would be a place you could reach by doing the right things in the right order.

Then time started to behave like time does, which is to say: without apology. People I knew moved away, stopped calling, or simply disappeared from my orbit without drama. Others stayed, and their staying became its own kind of marvel. My own plans didn’t collapse all at once. They bent, stretched, and recalibrated. I found myself adapting in ways that felt less like choosing and more like learning to swim.

It’s difficult to describe how learning to swim feels, especially if you’ve always been confident in dry land. At first, you fight the water. You treat it like an opponent. You strain for control and discover that control is mostly a fantasy. Then one day you realize you don’t have to defeat the water. You just have to move with it. You have to stop insisting that the current is wrong and start asking what direction it’s trying to take you.

There are people who tell you to trust yourself, as if that were as simple as deciding. But self-trust can be a trick. Sometimes it means you believe your worst impulses. Sometimes it means you ignore warning signs because your ego prefers a flattering story. Real trust takes practice. It looks more like paying attention than like affirming.

I’ve learned that paying attention is a form of courage. Not the dramatic kind, not the kind where you run into burning buildings. It’s smaller, quieter courage: noticing when you’ve been holding your breath. Recognizing when you’ve been pretending. Admitting you don’t know what you’re doing. Standing in the middle of uncertainty and refusing to lie about it.

The ocean is a good teacher of this kind of courage. It doesn’t explain itself. It doesn’t justify its tides. It simply does what it does, and in the doing, it makes a kind of truth out of consistency. If you watch long enough, you start to notice patterns. Even chaos repeats itself in ways that can be learned.

One afternoon, later in the same trip, I sat on the beach with my shoes kicked off, feeling the cool sand seep around my ankles. The day had warmed into something brighter. Families moved through the shoreline with buckets and towels. Children ran like the world had no gravity. A gull landed near me with the confidence of a creature that had never had to ask permission.

I had brought a book, but I didn’t open it. Instead, I listened. At first, “listening” felt like a passive act, like letting sound happen around you. But after a while, it became active. I began to hear the difference between a wave arriving and a wave leaving. I could sense the rhythm: the rush forward, the pause, the slow retreat. Underneath it, there was always the deeper motion, the ocean’s long breathing.

It occurred to me that we are all trying to be something like that—trying to have a rhythm. Trying to move forward and withdraw, forward and withdraw, without losing ourselves entirely in the currents.

The question is what we mean when we say “ourselves.” Is it the version of us that wants certainty? Is it the version that wants to be admired? Is it the version that believes in control? Or is it something more flexible—something that can be carried by the tide without being dragged under?

I think “self” is less like a fixed object and more like a current shape. It changes over time, but it retains certain characteristics. It’s recognizable. When I’m at my best, I feel like I’m in conversation with the world rather than fighting it. I’m responsive instead of rigid. I let experiences move through me instead of grabbing and clenching as though I could keep them forever.

This is what I took from that ocean day, though I didn’t have the words yet. The ocean showed me that vastness isn’t the same as distance. You can stand near something immense and still feel connected to it, not through ownership but through attention.

On the walk back, the sky was different again. The clouds had shifted, and the light now looked more decisive. In the water, blue returned, but it still carried those other colors inside it. The ocean never became only blue. It was always more complicated than the label.

Maybe that’s a lesson worth keeping: the world is rarely what our first word claims. People are like that too. We reduce each other to versions that are convenient. We say someone is “always” this way or “never” that way, and we build a small box around them. But the truth is that everyone changes depending on the light, on the weather of their days, on the invisible pressures moving through them.

So I try, imperfectly, to stay open. To let my own moods be something I observe rather than something that dictates every decision. To remember that my present state might be a tide, not a permanent sea.

When night came, the ocean continued. I didn’t need to watch it to know it was still doing what it had always done. There’s comfort in that—being able to trust a process you can’t see. Somewhere out there, the waves kept returning, not because they promised anything, but because returning was their nature.

And I think that’s what hope is, when it’s honest. Not a guarantee. Not a prediction. Just the willingness to believe that motion continues—that even if you can’t control the current, you can keep learning how to move with it.
